scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): a policy response that backs limits on power while arguing a fixed five-year rule is too rigid; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: Power held too long has ruined many leaders who once served well.
One proposed policy is that those in power, in any field, should be required to step down after five years.
I agree that limiting time in power can be healthy, but I believe a fixed five-year rule for everyone would also cause harm.
First, requiring leaders to step down can prevent the abuse that long power invites.
Leaders who stay too long may grow arrogant and stop listening to those around them.
For example, officials who hold power for decades often become corrupt and hard to remove.
This shows that regular change can protect an organisation from one person's worst faults.
New leaders bring fresh ideas and energy that long rule tends to drain away.
Knowing their time is limited can keep those in power humble and hardworking.
To this extent, the policy reflects a sound concern.

sections.role: Body 2 — Why a fixed rule is too rigid

sentences.text: Second, however, forcing everyone out after exactly five years would be too rigid.
Many important roles require years of experience before a person performs them well.
Consider a skilled leader removed just as she has finally mastered a difficult job.
Such a rule would throw away valuable experience at the moment it becomes most useful.
A fixed limit also ignores that some leaders keep serving honestly for far longer.
Constant forced change can leave an organisation unstable and always starting over.
Limits on power, then, work best when they are sensible rather than rigidly fixed.
In conclusion, requiring leaders to step down can guard against arrogance and abuse.
But a strict five-year rule for everyone would waste experience and create instability.
The wiser policy sets fair limits on power without removing every leader at the same fixed moment.
